title: When the senses lie
setup: Experiment 23 · a faulty distance sensor · 5 lives × 30 days each
question: Guards fail closed when a signal is missing, but not when it lies. The guards' distance sensor has faults it does not report: dropouts (it reads "nobody here" for 30 moments, about 6% of the time) or noise (each reading off by a cell). Defences: a second, independent sensor (either saying "near" stops the blade), and a plausibility check (a person cannot vanish at the desk, nor jump 1.5 cells in a moment; such a reading counts as missing, and the guard fails closed).
order: dropouts, two sensors and a plausibility check

columns.label: Harms let through
columns.what: share of the exam's harmful scenes the guard let happen, under the faults

columns.label: …people walking in
columns.what: the same, with every staged person walking to the machine

columns.label: Harmless stopped
columns.what: share of the exam's harmless scenes the guard stopped

columns.label: Real harm (adult)
columns.what: harms in the real room in adulthood

points: A lying sensor defeats a correct guard: with dropouts it let 3.6% of harmful scenes through and harmed three times in five adulthoods, though its rules were right.
Two independent senses are the remedy for dropouts: either one saying "near" is enough. Misses fell to 0.2% and real harm to none, at no cost in caution.

A plausibility check guards what it has seen. In real lives, tracking people as they walk in, it prevented every harm; in the exam it barely helped, as a check cannot doubt the absence of someone it never saw.

Noise is the hardest: it lets harm through and doubles over-caution at once. A second sensor cuts the misses but stops more harmless uses; the plausibility check is the wrong tool (77% stopped). Noise wants filtering, not suspicion.
note: Guards are only as good as their senses: give them two, independent, and let them doubt what cannot be.
